text:
“Come, come,” she said to me, “drive away those bad theories and laugh; life is delightful, my dear, depending on the glass through which one looks at it. Here, consult your friend Gaston; there is a man who strikes me as understanding love as I understand it. What you must be convinced of, unless you want to become an insipid young man, is that next door there is a beautiful girl who is impatiently waiting for the man who is with her to leave, who is thinking of you, who is reserving her night for you, and who loves you—I am certain of it. Now come and stand at the window with me, and let us watch the count leave; he will not be long in making room for us.”

Prudence opened a window, and we leaned side by side on the balcony.

She watched the few passersby; I dreamed.

Everything she had said was buzzing in my head, and I could not help admitting that she was right; but the genuine love I felt for Marguerite had difficulty accommodating itself to that reasoning. And so, from time to time, I heaved sighs that made Prudence turn around and shrug her shoulders like a doctor who has despaired of a patient.

“How clearly one perceives that life must be short,” I said to myself, “from the rapidity of its sensations! I have known Marguerite for only two days, she has been my mistress only since yesterday, and she has already so completely taken possession of my thoughts, my heart, and my life that this visit from the Count de G... is a calamity for me.”

At last the count came out, got back into his carriage, and disappeared. Prudence closed her window.

At that same moment Marguerite called us.

“Come quickly, they are setting the table,” she said. “We are going to have supper.”

When I entered her rooms, Marguerite ran to me, threw herself upon my neck, and kissed me with all her might.

“Are we still sulking?” she asked me.

“No, it is over,” Prudence replied. “I gave him a moral lecture, and he promised to behave.”

“That is more like it!”

In spite of myself, I glanced at the bed; it was still made. As for Marguerite, she was already wearing a white dressing gown.

We sat down at table.

Charm, sweetness, openness—Marguerite had them all, and from time to time I was forced to acknowledge that I had no right to ask anything more of her; that many people would have been happy in my place; and that, like Virgil’s shepherd, I had only to enjoy the leisure a god—or rather a goddess—afforded me.

I tried to put Prudence’s theories into practice and to be as cheerful as my two companions; but what was natural in them was an effort in me, and my nervous laughter, which deceived them, came very close to tears.

At last supper came to an end, and I was left alone with Marguerite. As was her habit, she went and sat on her rug before the fire and gazed sadly at the flame in the hearth.

She was musing! About what? I do not know. I watched her lovingly and almost fearfully as I thought of what I was ready to suffer for her.

“Dost thou know what I was thinking about?”

“No.”

“About a plan I have devised.”

“And what is this plan?”

“I cannot confide it to thee yet, but I can tell thee what would result from it. The result would be that a month from now I should be free, I should no longer owe anything, and we should go and spend the summer together in the country.”

“And you cannot tell me by what means?”

“No; thou needst only love me as I love thee, and everything will succeed.”

“And did you devise this plan entirely by yourself?”

“Yes.”

“And will you carry it out by yourself?”

“I alone shall have the troubles,” Marguerite said to me with a smile I shall never forget, “but we shall share the profits.”

I could not help blushing at the word “profits”; I remembered Manon Lescaut and Des Grieux living on M. de B...’s money.

I replied in a rather harsh tone, rising as I did so:

“You will permit me, my dear Marguerite, to share only in the profits of ventures that I devise and carry out myself.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means that I strongly suspect the Count de G... of being your partner in this happy plan, whose liabilities and profits I accept neither.”

“You are a child. I thought you loved me; I was mistaken. Very well.”

At the same time, she rose, opened her piano, and began playing the Invitation to the Dance again, up to that famous passage in the major key that always stopped her.

Was it from habit, or to remind me of the day on which we had met? All I know is that with that melody my memories returned, and, going over to her, I took her head between my hands and kissed her.

“Do you forgive me?” I asked her.

“You can plainly see that I do,” she replied; “but take note that this is only our second day, and already I have something to forgive you for. You keep your promises of blind obedience very badly.”

“What can I do, Marguerite? I love you too much, and I am jealous of your slightest thought. What you proposed to me just now would drive me wild with joy, but the mystery preceding the execution of this plan constricts my heart.”

“Come, let us reason a little,” she resumed, taking both my hands and looking at me with a charming smile that I found impossible to resist. “You love me, do you not? And you would be happy to spend three or four months in the country alone with me. I too would be happy in that solitude together; not only would I be happy in it, but I need it for my health. I cannot leave Paris for so long without putting my affairs in order, and the affairs of a woman like me are always very tangled. Well, I have found the means of reconciling everything—my affairs and my love for you; yes, for you, do not laugh: I am mad enough to love you! And now you put on your grand airs and say grand words to me. Child, child three times over, remember only that I love you, and do not worry about anything.—Is it agreed, then?”

“Whatever you want is agreed; you know that very well.”

“Then, before a month has passed, we shall be in some village, walking beside the water and drinking milk. It seems strange to you that I, Marguerite Gautier, should speak in this way. That is because, my friend, when this Parisian life, which seems to make me so happy, does not consume me, it bores me, and then I have sudden yearnings for a quieter existence that would remind me of my childhood. One has always had a childhood, whatever one may have become. Oh! Do not worry, I am not going to tell you that I am the daughter of a retired colonel and that I was educated at Saint-Denis. I am a poor country girl, and six years ago I did not know how to write my name. That reassures you, does it not? Why are you the first person to whom I turn to share the joy of the desire that came over me? No doubt because I recognized that you loved me for my sake and not for yours, whereas the others have never loved me except for their own.”
